abstract.p: This study reports the flexible synthesis of syn-anti isomers of highly functionalized tetrahydropyridines under controlled temperature conditions. The present catalytic system employs cost-effective meso-2,3-dibromosuccinic acid in a one-pot, multicomponent process involving both aromatic aldehydes, anilines, and 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds to produce a structurally diverse tetrahydropyridines. The current catalyst, meso-2,3-dibromosuccinic acid, demonstrates a unique capability for selective synthesis of syn:anti tetrahydropyridine isomers. Unlike other reported catalysts, it enables exclusive formation of the syn isomer at low temperatures (5 °C) and allows tunable syn:anti ratios at moderate temperatures (25 °C). Moreover, at 65 °C, meso-2,3-dibromosuccinic acid exclusively yields the anti isomer highlighting its distinct advantage in controlling product selectivity. Other notable features of this method include simple work-up procedure, the absence of transition metal catalysts, high structural diversity of the products, and excellent product yields. Thermodynamics, kinetics, aromaticity, frontier orbitals, and 1H NMR in gas, ethanol, and chloroform phase at different temperature are studied using density functional theory. According to the thermodynamics, aromaticity and energy gap results the anti isomer is more stable than syn one, but the latter have lower activation energy than the former, therefore, the rate constant of formation of syn isomer is several times of anti form at low temperatures.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In recent decades, the synthesis of chiral heterocyclic molecules—particularly diastereomeric compounds—via multicomponent coupling reactions has drawn significant attention from organic and medicinal chemists1–3. These chiral molecules are widely found in numerous biologically active, pharmaceutical, agrochemical, and industrial compounds4, making their efficient synthesis and separation a major focus in modern organic chemistry5–7.

Nitrogen-containing heterocycle molecules represent an extremely important class of heterocyclic compounds, widely found in drugs, vitamins, and various natural and biologically active compounds8,9. They are also used as ligands and sensors due to their bioactivity10–16.

Recently, among the nitrogen-containing heterocycles, tetrahydropyridines and their analogues have attracted considerable attention due to their diverse biological and pharmacological activities, such as anti-hypertensive17, anti-bacterial18, anti-malarial19, anti-inflammatory20, norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor21, neuro-protective22, PARP inhibition with antioxidant properties23, M5-preferring muscarinic receptor orthosteric antagonists24, and MP-MUS anti-cancer activity against human glioma cells25. Notably, they are also widely found in natural products26 and many clinically approved synthetic drugs incorporating the tetrahydropyridine or piperidine core exhibit chirality and are represented in Fig. 1. Moreover, approximately 50% of well-known alkaloids contain the piperidine core which plays a vital role in the biosynthesis of natural compounds27. they are also widely found in natural products.Fig. 1
Representative biologically and pharmaceutically active natural and synthetic tetrahydropyridines and piperidine derivatives.

Common methods for the synthesis of tetrahydropyridines involve aza-Prins-cyclizations28, imino Diels–Alder reactions29,30, intramolecular Mannich reaction onto iminium ions31, intramolecular aza-Michael reactions32, and cyclopropane ring-opening/Conia-ene cyclization33. A significant challenge associated with these synthetic routes is the lack of control over the syn:anti isomer ratio, which remains unpredictable and often limits the selectivity and efficiency of the process. In addition to these well-established routes, multicomponent reactions (MCRs) have also emerged as a valuable synthetic strategy for the preparation of tetrahydropyridines. In the past two decades, besides parallel synthesis and combinatorial synthetic approaches, the concept of MCRs has significantly inspired the scientific community. This versatile approach is particularly important compared to multi-step syntheses because of their one-step, high-efficiency, energy-saving, environmentally friendly, and their ability to synthesize large or small drug-like molecules34–43.

In this regard, various homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts such as InCl344, I245, bromodimethylsulfonium bromide (BDMS)46, ZrOCl2.8H2O47, Fe/MWCNTs48, Fe3O4@TDSN-Bi(III)49, cerium ammonium nitrate (CAN)50, acetic acid51, graphene oxide52, L-proline nitrate53, oxalic acid54, tetrabutylammonium tribromide (TBATB)55, chromium(III)-salen complex nanoparticles on AlPO456, nanomagnetic organic–inorganic hybrid (Fe@Si-Gu-Prs)57, cyanuric chloride58, RB@ZIF-859, and Fe3O4@Dop/CP-diPy-ZnCl260 have been reported for the synthesis of polysubstituted tetrahydropyridines61,62 with a predominant formation of the anti-isomer. However, these methods sometimes suffer from severe drawbacks such as the use of a metals, harsh reaction conditions, low stereoselectivity and product contamination. Therefore, a metal-free and mild protocol for the synthesis of highly substituted tetrahydropyridines using simple and readily available starting materials and catalyst is highly exigent.

In 2011, Mukhopadhyay and co-workers reported the formation of a syn-diastereoisomer in the diastereoselective synthesis of highly functionalized piperidines catalysed by wet picric acid63. Notably, this pioneering work represents the first reported example of a selective synthesis of the syn/anti-diastereoisomer in the diastereoselective synthesis of tetrahydropyridines, with no other such reports available in the literature to date. Such highlights encouraged us to delve into the development of a more selective catalytic system, aiming to remove the obstacles associated with diastereoselectivity and control of the syn:anti ratio of tetrahydropyridines. By exploring novel catalytic systems and reaction conditions, we sought to expand the scope of tetrahydropyridine synthesis while enhancing yield, selectivity, and sustainability.

In light of the above and as a part of our recent interest in the multicomponent synthesis of nitrogen-containing heterocycles64,65, especially tetrahydropyridine compounds66–70, we herein disclose a facile and atom-economical methodology for the direct and stereoselective synthesis of tetrahydropyridines through five-component reaction of aromatic aldehydes (2.0 equiv.), aromatic amines (2.0 equiv.), and methyl/ethyl acetoacetate (1.0 equiv.) with controllable distereoselectivity and a temperature-controlled ratio of syn:anti. In the presence of only a low catalytic amount of the catalyst, the newly developed catalytic system proceeds with high distereoselectivity and broad substrate scope under mild conditions.

sec.title: Results and discussion
sec.p:
At the outset of this study, a model reaction was conducted using benzaldehyde (2.0 mmol), aniline (2.0 mmol), methyl acetoacetate (1.0 mmol) in ethanol at different temperatures (5 °C, 25 °C, and 65 °C) in the presence of various catalysts for the synthesis of tetrahydropyridine 4 (Table 1). The study commenced using PrCl3.6H2O as a catalyst in EtOH at 5 °C, 25 °C, 65 °C, which led to the formation of desired pure anti isomer of tetrahydropyridine 4a′ (entry 1). Interestingly, meso-2,3-dibromosuccinic acid exhibits strong temperature-dependent behavior. When meso-2,3-dibromosuccinic acid was used as a catalyst, it provides complete selectivity for the syn isomer (4a) at 5 °C in EtOH (entry 2). As the temperature increases to 25 °C, the ratio shifts to ~ 60:40, and at 65 °C, only the anti-isomer (4a′) is obtained in EtOH. Other examined Lewis and Bronsted acid catalysts (entries 3–11) exclusively favor the formation of the anti product across all tested temperatures in ethanol solvent. Moreover, p-phenolsulfonic acid also demonstrates temperature-dependent selectivity, with a 45:55 ratio at 5 °C, which shifts to 21:79 at 25 °C, and ultimately results in complete anti selectivity at 65 °C (entry 4). Control runs with no catalyst present showed no conversion (entry 12). The effect of solvents on the reaction outcome was also examined in the presence of meso-2,3-dibromosuccinic acid. In methanol, the anti-product is exclusively formed at all temperatures. In both THF and acetonitrile, diastereoselectivity shifts toward the anti-isomer as the temperature increases, with complete anti selectivity (0:100) observed at 65 °C. These results confirm that the temperature plays a crucial role in the syn-anti ratios of tetrahydropyridines 4. Also, we investigated the effect of non-polar solvents such as chloroform, diethyl ether, ethyl acetate, and methylene chloride on the catalytic reaction (Table 1, entries 16–19). In non-polar solvents such as chloroform, diethyl ether, and dichloromethane at 5 °C, the desired product was not obtained. When ethyl acetate was used as the solvent at 5 °C, a mixture of syn and anti isomers with a ratio of 20:80 was produced. Furthermore, we evaluated the effect of different catalyst loadings, 2, 4, 7, and 11 mol%, and the overall yield was less than 15 mol% (Table 1, entries 20–23). In addition, the model reaction was tested at additional temperatures of 0, 35, and 50 °C. At 0 °C, an obtained syn isomer was obtained with 45% yield. Anti-isomer was formed at 35 and 50 °C in 53 and 65% yield, respectively.

Finally, the reaction was investigated at − 15 °C but the desired product was not observed. After achieving the optimized reaction conditions, the scope of the reaction was explored with various aldehydes and amines, having electron-donating and withdrawing substrates as well as methyl or ethyl acetoacetate in the presence of meso-2,3-dibromosuccinic acid as the chosen catalyst. The results are shown in Table 2. Initially, the reaction between benzaldehyde, aniline, and methyl acetoacetate led to the formation of the syn diastereomer of tetrahydropyridine 4a (Table 2, entry 1). The diastereomeric ratio (syn:anti) of tetrahydropyridine 4 was determined using 1H-NMR spectroscopy. This was achieved by analyzing the distinct chemical shifts and J-coupling constants of key protons, including NH, C2–H, C6–H, and C5–H′ protons (Scheme 1). The C6–H [δ: 4.56 (dd, J = 12.0, 4.0 Hz, 1H, H-6)] and C2–H [δ: 6.19 (s, 1H, H-2)] protons of the syn-isomer are shifted compared to those of the anti-isomer [C6–H, δ: 5.19 (d, J = 2.5 Hz, 1H, H-6) and C2-H, δ: 6.51 (s, 1H, H-2)]. Additionally, the C5–H′ [δ: 2.46 (dd, J = 12.0, 16.0 Hz, 1H, H′-5)] of the syn isomer is more shielded than that of the anti-isomer [δ: 2.80 (dd, J = 15.0, 2.5 Hz, 1H, H′-5)]. Moreover, the NH (δ: 10.64) proton of the syn isomer is deshielded compared to that of anti-isomer (δ: 10.31). Halogenated anilines underwent a smooth condensation reaction with 2-methylbenzaldehyde and methyl acetoacetate to afford the corresponding syn isomers in 55, 67, and 60% yields, respectively (Table 2, entries 5–7).
Next, anilines with electron-donating groups at the para position such as Me and OMe were investigated in this reaction and desired syn products were successfully obtained (Table 2, entries 8–9).

Gratifyingly, 2,6-di-chlorobenzldehyde, a highly sterically hindered substrate worked well in this protocol, leading to the selective synthesis of syn isomers (Table 2, entries 10–11). Notably, the reaction of benzaldehydes bearing electron-donating groups at the para position such as -Me, -isopropyl, and -OMe (entries 12–21) exclusively yielded the anti isomer indicating a significant shift in stereochemical preference compared to earlier entries where the syn isomer predominated. The impact of halogen substituents at the ortho and para position of aldehyde on the stereochemical outcome of the reaction was also investigated. When R1 was taken to be halogens (Cl, Br, and F), the reaction proceeded with complete diastereoselectivity, exclusively yielding the anti-isomer of 4v′−x′ products in high yields (entries 22–24). Further, it was found that the reaction of heterocyclic aldehydes such as 2-pyridinecarboxaldehyde with 4-chloroaniline and methyl acetoacetate resulted in the formation of product tetrahydropyridine (4y′) in 60% yield (entry 25). Copies of 1H, 13C, and 19F NMR spectra (Figs. S7–S60) are provided in the Supplementary Information file.

To support the proposed mechanism, several control reactions were performed (Scheme 2). Initially, benzaldehyde (1a) was allowed to react with aniline (2a) in ethanol under catalytic conditions at both 5 and 65 °C, affording the corresponding imine (2aa) in 74% and 80% yields, respectively (Scheme 2, I)71.Scheme 2
Control experiments (I–III).

Subsequently, under identical conditions, the condensation of aniline (2a) with methyl acetoacetate (3) was carried out, providing the expected enamine (3aa) in 78% and 86% yields at 5 and 65 °C, respectively (Scheme 2, II)72,73 Finally, the imine (2aa) generated in the first step was subjected to reaction with the enamine (3aa) obtained in the second step and benzaldehyde (1a) under the standard conditions, affording the corresponding syn and anti products in 72% and 83% yields, respectively (Scheme 2, III).

Based on previous reports46,47,63,69,74,75, a possible mechanistic pathway for the preparation of syn and anti isomers of tetrahydropyridines in the presence of meso-2,3-dibromosuccinic acid as an acid catalyst is proposed (Scheme 3).Scheme 3
The proposed reaction mechanism for syn and anti production. Initially, aniline (A) reacts with activated β-ketoester (B) in the presence of the catalyst producing enamine intermediate (C). This is followed by the formation of intermediate (E) through a Knoevenagel condensation between intermediate (C) and benzaldehyde (D). Subsequently, the diene intermediate (F) is obtained from the tautomerization process of Knoevenagel intermediate (E). Meanwhile, benzaldehyde and aniline react together to synthesis imine forms (G). Eventually, the diene intermediate (F) undergoes an aza-Diels–Alder reaction with the imine (G), leading to the formation of syn and anti isomers of the final tetrahydropyridine.

We propose a six-membered chair-like transition state for the Diels–Alder reaction between intermediates F and G (Scheme 4). In this model, the dienophile is an imine derived from aromatic aldehydes, and the nature and position of the substituents on the aryl ring influence the stereochemical outcome of the reaction. Imines derived from aldehydes bearing less sterically demanding substituents—such as para-substituted arenes—can approach the diene in a manner that allows the aryl group to occupy the axial position in the resulting tetrahydropyridine product. This axial positioning leads to an anti-relationship relative to the substituent at position 2 of the ring (Scheme 4a). In contrast, imines bearing bulkier aryl substituents, particularly in the ortho position, experience greater steric repulsion within the transition state. To minimize this interaction, these systems adopt a conformation in which the bulky aryl group is oriented away from the diene system, positioned outside the forming six-membered ring. As a result, the aryl group ends up preferentially in the equatorial position in the final product, thereby minimizing 1,3-diaxial interactions with axial hydrogens at position 2—ultimately favoring formation of the syn isomer as the major product (Scheme 4b). Notably, 2-chlorobenzaldehyde and 2-bromobenzaldehyde, although ortho-substituted, exhibit less steric hindrance than 2-methylbenzaldehyde. As a result, they are able to adopt an axial orientation in the final product, yielding the anti-isomer as the major species (entries 22, 23). These stereochemical outcomes are in good agreement with their relatively low conformational free energy values (− ΔGc), further supporting the proposed mechanistic rationale76,77.Scheme 4
Propose a six-membered chair-like transition state for the Diels–Alder reaction between intermediates F and G.

In the case of imines derived from 2-pyridinecarboxaldehyde, which lack bulky ortho substituents, the reaction predominantly yields the anti-isomer. This outcome can be rationalized by the ability of the unsubstituted pyridine ring to adopt an axial orientation in the chair-like transition state. The absence of steric hindrance allows the heteroaryl ring to align more closely with the diene system, favoring a transition state in which the pyridyl group occupies the axial position, ultimately leading to the formation of the anti product (Table 2, entry 25).

In the context of Diels–Alder cyclization, the reaction can proceed via different trajectories for the diene and dienophile (Scheme 5). As illustrated in Scheme 5, among the four possible approaches (1–4), steps 1 and 2 are more favorable. In the exo approach, the two molecules, imine (II) and diene (I) can be directly on top of each other; one molecule appears to be folded underneath the other. This approach typically results in the formation of the syn isomer, whereas the endo approach leads to the more stable anti isomer.Scheme 5

sec.title: Theory and methodology
Thermodynamics and kinetics study
sec.p:
As mentioned above based on Scheme 3, reaction between the diene intermediate (F) undergoes an aza-Diels–Alder reaction with the imine (G) leading to the foundation of syn and anti isomers of the final tetrahydropyridine. Therefore, here, we optimized the diene, imine, their TSs between them which causes the syn and anti isomers (named; TS-syn and TS-anti, respectively), syn and anti molecules in gas and ethanol phase by B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) level of theory (see Tables S1, S2 and Figs. S1, S2). All the stated molecules were characterized by vibrational analysis to confirm the real minima and ensured that the TS-syn and TS-anti geometries had a single imaginary frequency. As seen in both gas and ethanol phase and in all three different temperatures (5 °C, 25 °C, and 65 °C) the anti isomer is more stable than syn one. These results are also seen in the chloroform phase (see Table S3). In addition, it seen that the TS-syn is more stable than TS-anti in both gas and ethanol phase which is also their existence and stability are confirmed by M06-2X/6-31G(d,p) level of theory (see Table S4 and Fig. S3). Consequently, the activation energy (Ea) of TS-syn is less than TS-anti in both gas and ethanol phase and it creates a kinetic competition between the syn and anti isomers as obtained in Table S5 and see in Fig. 2. As can be obtained the rate constant ratio of syn and anti isomers in three different mentioned temperatures in gas phase are 248, 211, and 129, respectively, and in ethanol phase these ratios are 548, 420, and 251, respectively. This calculation shows that the rate of formation of syn isomer is much faster than anti isomer at low temperatures as anticipated by Mukhopadhyay et al. “syn formation is favored due to kinetic control and lower activation energy, whereas at higher temperatures, the system undergoes thermodynamic equilibration, leading to the preferential formation of the anti-product”63.Fig. 2
Relative potential energy diagram of the imine and diene reaction and transition states and their resulting products (anti and syn) with activation energies, Ea, in gas (red line) and ethanol (blue line) phase obtained by B3LYP/6-31 g(d,p) level of theory.

By calculating the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy gap, ΔE, we can determine the kinetic stability, chemical reactivity, optical polarizability, and chemical hardness–softness of a molecule. The ΔE explains the eventual charge transfer interaction within the molecule, which influences the biological activity of the molecule. A large ΔE indicates high kinetic stability and low chemical reactivity, because it is energetically undesirable to draw out electrons from a HOMO and enhance electrons to a LUMO, and so to construct the activated complex of any potential reaction97,98. From Figs. S4 and S5 it is achieved that ΔE of syn isomer in gas and ethanol phase, 6.50 eV and 6.44 eV, respectively, is a little more than anti form, 6.23 eV, and 6.12 eV, respectively, which shows that the former kinetically is more stable than the latter, and the anti isomer chemically is more reactive than the syn form.

To further study the stability of anti and syn molecules, the aromaticity of the central ring (the pyridine ring) was investigated. As seen in Table S6 all of the four aromaticity indices of calculated NICSs (NICS(0), NICS(0)zz, NICS(1), and NICS(1)zz), in gas, ethanol, and chloroform phase represented that the pyridine rings in both anti and syn form are non/anti aromatic with the different that pyridine ring in anti molecule is a little more aromatic than in syn one. Accordingly, it seems that anti isomer is more stable than syn form which also in line with HOMO–LUMO energy gap.

sec.title: Comparative theoretical and experimental 1H NMR
sec.p: Figure S6 reveal the calculation of 1H NMR of anti and sym molecules (ppm) in gas and chloroform phase using GIAO/B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) method. Besides, Table S7 shows the comparison between experimental and calculated of the selected hydrogen chemical shifts (N–H, C2–H, C6–H, C5–H′, and C5–H″) of anti and sym molecules in gas and chloroform phase. As can be seen in both gas and chloroform phase the calculated N–H chemical shift of syn isomer (11.80, and 11.54, respectively) is shifted compared to that of anti form (11.39, and 11.29, respectively) which is consistent with the experimental results (δ N–H of syn, and anti molecules are 10.64, and 10.31, respectively). The calculated C2–H chemical shift of anti isomer in gas and chloroform (6.54, and 6.68, respectively), and that of syn form (5.21, and 5.48, respectively) are close to the experimental results (6.51, and 6.19 in anti and syn isomers, respectively). It can be seen that the achieved values of proton shift for C5–H′ and C5–H″ in gas phase are close to those of experimental compared to the chloroform phase. Despite the difference in solvent in the experimental (CDCl3), and theoretical cases, the results obtained are satisfactory.

sec.title: General information
sec.p: All reagents and solvents were obtained from commercial sources like Merck, Sigma-Aldrich, and Fluka. All known products were identified by comparison of their spectral data and melting points with those of the valid samples. 1H NMR (250 and 400 MHz) and 13C NMR (62.5 and 100 MHz), spectra were recorded on Brucker Avance DRX. Melting points were checked by a Büchi B-545 apparatus in open capillary tubes. All reactions were monitored by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) using silica gel plates (silica gel 60 F254 Merck Chemical Company). The elemental analysis was performed using a PerkinElmer 240-B microanalyzer.

General Procedure for the synthesis of syn and anti isomers of tetrahydropyridines 4: A solution of β-ketoester (1.0 mmol) and aromatic amine (2.0 mmol) in EtOH (5 mL) was stirred for 30 min in the presence of 15 mol% meso-2,3-dibromosuccinic acid at 5 °C temperature. Next, the aromatic aldehyde (2.0 mmol) was added to the reaction mixture. After completion of the reaction (monitored by thin-layer chromatography), the thick precipitate was filtered off and washed with EtOH (3 × 2 mL) to achieve the pure product.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In the present study, the meso-2,3-dibromosuccinic acid as a robust and cost-effective catalyst was employed for the preparation of selective syn isomer of tetrahydropyridines through a multicomponent reaction between aldehydes, amines, and 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds. A key challenge in such syntheses is the low diastereoselectivity for the syn:anti ratio. However, the current catalyst overcomes this limitation by enabling exclusive formation of the syn isomer at low temperatures (5 °C). Notably, at 65 °C, it selectively yields the anti isomer, highlighting its distinct advantage in controlling product selectivity. Additional benefits of this method include an easy work-up system, metal-free conditions, and high stereoselectivity with relatively high yields in low temperature. DFT studies [B3LYP and M06-2X with 6-31 g(d,p)] in gas and ethanol phases confirmed the proposed mechanism. The TS-syn structure showed lower activation energy and higher kinetic favorability than TS-anti, explaining the predominant formation of the syn isomer at low temperature. Although the anti isomer is thermodynamically more stable, the syn isomer has a slightly larger HOMO–LUMO gap, indicating greater kinetic stability. NICS aromaticity indices revealed non/anti-aromatic pyridine rings in both isomers, with the anti form being slightly more aromatic, consistent with thermodynamic data. The calculated 1H NMR spectra of both isomers matched the experimental results.
